newsitem.title: INDIA: Gold - Indian sub-continent prices seen mixed.
newsitem.headline: Gold - Indian sub-continent prices seen mixed.

text.p: Gold prices in the Indian subcontinent are expected to be mixed in the near-term with imports pressuring Indian markets but political turmoil expected to push Pakistani prices higher, dealers said on Monday.
They said a subdued trend in world gold prices, sparked by a recent slide in silver, may lead to higher gold imports into India.
On the Bombay bullion market, standard gold (24 carats) climbed a modest 15 rupees per 10 grammes to 5,120 rupees in the week to Monday.
"Restricted supplies helped gold prices rise slightly but I expect fresh arrivals in the coming days because of an easy trend in the world market," said dealer Bhayabhai Sanghvi.
Indian dealers also see a lull in demand for gold in the next two weeks before it picks up for major Hindu festivals in October and November.

In Karachi, Pakistan's main commercial city, dealers predicted gold prices would rise this week on demand prompted by fears of more turmoil after the killing of Murtaza Bhutto, the estranged brother of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto.
Dealers said people were switching to gold from equities as a hedge against political and economic volatility.
Murtaza Bhutto's death on Friday during a shoot-out with police has already triggered violent protests from his supporters in Pakistan's Sind province.
"Gold rates will rise as major stocks players have taken losses and are looking for a safer investment," said a dealer.
Gold prices rose last week following a 3.79 percent devaluation of the Pakistani rupee against the dollar by the State (central) Bank of Pakistan on September 10.
In Dubai, the feeder market for demand in the Indian sub-continent, gold imports dropped in August.
According to the World Gold Council, gold imports into the Gulf Arab emirate fell 1.04 tonnes to 28.848 tonnes during the month.
The figures coincide with a seasonal downturn in trade because of the harsh Gulf summer, which caps business as expatriates and Gulf nationals take vacations.
Nearly 80 percent of Dubai's gold imports are re-exported to the Indian subcontinent, mostly to India, the world's single largest gold consumer.
"Shipments to India are going very well. Demand is not depressed there," a regular supplier to India said.
